text: You're given an integer array nums and an integer k. Split nums into k non-empty contiguous subarrays, so that the largest subarray sum is as small as possible. Return that minimized largest sum.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the pieces have to be contiguous. So I'm not choosing which elements go together; I'm only choosing where to put the cuts. With n elements there are n minus one gaps, and I pick k minus one of them. Are there any constraints on the input size?
n is up to a thousand. Each value is between zero and ten to the sixth. And k is at most the smaller of fifty and n.

Good — all values are non-negative. I'll come back to that, because it's what makes my whole approach work. Let me think about the answer itself for a sec. It can never be smaller than the max element, since that element sits in some piece. And it can never be bigger than the total sum, since one single piece is always an option. So the answer lives between the max and the sum. On the example, seven, two, five, ten, eight with k equals two: max is ten, sum is thirty-two. Cutting after the five gives sums fourteen and eighteen, so the largest is eighteen. Any other single cut is worse.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would try every way to place the cuts — n minus one choose k minus one, which is astronomically large for a thousand elements and fifty pieces. The next step up is a DP that tries every spot for the last cut. That's k times n squared, about five times ten to the seventh. It works, but it's slow and fiddly. This problem reminds me of binary search on the answer. Asking for the best split is hard. But asking how few pieces I need if I cap every piece at v is one greedy pass. So I flip the optimization into a yes-or-no question and binary search on v. The trade-off: the DP gives the cut positions, binary search only gives the value — but the value is all the problem asks for.

Here's the plan. One: search the cap between the max and the sum — both ends are real splits. Two: for each cap, walk left to right with a running sum, cut whenever the next element would pass the cap, and count the pieces. Three: if that count is at most k, keep the cap and go left; otherwise step past it. Two things make this correct. Greedy really gives the fewest pieces, because pushing an early cut later never makes a later piece heavier. And the test is monotone: if a cap works, any bigger cap works, so I want the first true. One thing worth flagging: the test is at most k, not exactly k. Extra cuts only shrink pieces, and exactly k would break the monotone shape. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
That sounds good. Go ahead and code it.

Alright, let me code this up. The main loop squeezes left and right toward the first feasible cap, and a helper counts pieces greedily. One thing worth flagging is the reset in that helper: when x doesn't fit, I zero cur and count a new piece first, then add x, because x belongs to the new piece. Drop the reset and cur becomes a prefix sum — on seven, nine, five with k equals two it returns sixteen instead of fourteen. And because left starts at the max, every cap fits any single element, so I never need a separate check. Starting at zero instead would make six, seven with k equals two return six instead of seven.

Let's dry-run the code with seven, two, five, ten, eight and k equals two, starting from ten and thirty-two. Round three is the interesting one. At eighteen, the second piece is ten plus eight, exactly at the cap. That still counts as feasible, because my test is strictly greater, not greater or equal. Then seventeen splits into three pieces, so left moves up and the answer is eighteen. That matches. Corner cases: a single seven with k equals one returns seven without looping. One, four, four with k equals three gives four, each element alone. All zeros gives zero. Two, zero, zero, three with k equals two gives three — zeros never force a cut.

Time is n log S, where S is the total sum: each greedy pass is linear, and the range halves every round. Space is constant. In the worst case the range is about ten to the ninth wide, so about thirty rounds — roughly three times ten to the fourth operations, versus five times ten to the seventh for the DP. Let me think about overflow here. The sum tops out at ten to the ninth, and int max is about two point one times ten to the ninth, so int is safe, but only by about two times. With bigger inputs I'd switch to long long. Oh, one more thing — this all rests on non-negative values. With negatives, greedy stops being optimal: four, four, minus four with a cap of four takes two greedy pieces, but one piece is enough. Then I'd fall back to the DP.

Nice work. Three things stood out. You bounded the answer before choosing an algorithm, and that same lower bound turned out to be what keeps your feasibility check correct — you proved it with six, seven. You caught that at most k and exactly k aren't interchangeable, and gave the real reason: exactly k breaks the monotone shape binary search depends on. And you named the assumption your solution rests on — non-negative values — with a concrete three-element array where the greedy breaks.
